correctness.rationale: For each JR violation an unelected candidate has q uncovered supporters. Optimal welfare and max column degree imply each selected candidate has precisely q supporters. Since kq>=n but the q uncovered supporters leave at most n-q represented vertices, one selected candidate has overlapping support, so a degree-neutral swap improves coverage by at least one. No 2-cohesive group exists at maximum support q, hence JR implies EJR. There are at most n swaps. The explicit q+1 family gives a unique welfare maximizer with a JR violation and exact one-welfare-unit remedy; all q>=1. Exhaustive verifier checked 1,803,670 small election-size instances and 100 sharpness parameters, supporting but not replacing the proof.

originality.rationale: A column-degree bound at the Hare quota ensures that a lexicographically welfare/coverage optimal committee satisfies EJR, with a strictly coverage-improving welfare-neutral swap and an exactly sharp q+1 counterexample family. The nearest inspected papers establish unrestricted hardness (Dong 2026), generic welfare-loss bounds (Elkind et al. 2024), or interval-domain algorithms (Schünke 2026), not the sharp column-degree boundary. A prior result assumes at most two approvals per voter and fixed k=3, an incomparable row-degree domain. Equivalence cannot be ruled out globally; searchable literature did not reveal the claim.
residual_risks: Unindexed or differently worded low-frequency set-cover/maximum-coverage exchange lemmas may imply the result.
Foundational Aziz et al. (2017) article was not independently inspected in complete full text; only definitions and citations were checked via other full papers.
Semantic retrieval does not exhaust all published findings or guarantee novelty.
The result is restricted to standard EJR and dichotomous additive welfare; stronger EJR+ and instance-specific behavior above the cutoff remain open.

value.rationale: Sharp, structurally motivated zero-price EJR condition in a generally computationally hard welfare/representation problem. It holds over all committee sizes, arbitrary ballot lengths and all finite profiles under one natural maximum-candidate-support cap, and has a constructive polynomial-time tie-breaking algorithm. The q+1 examples prove exact uniform sharpness and give a meaningful first failure just outside the tractable domain, beyond mere reparametrization of bounded-per-voter approvals.
